newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH CNB SAYS CZK 90 BLN SPENT ON BANKING REVIVAL.
newsitem.headline: CZECH CNB SAYS CZK 90 BLN SPENT ON BANKING REVIVAL.

text.p: The Czech National Bank (CNB) said it had spent an estimated 90 billion crowns into programmes for consolidating troubled banks.

The CNB said in a report to the parliament that about 60 billion of the total costs were used in the first consolidation plan which included transfers of old bad loans to Konsolidacni Banka and recapitalisation of the large banks from 1991-1993.

A further 30 billion crowns were used since 1994 in the second programme in which several small banks were closed down or taken over by the CNB, and when central bank compensated clients above the level of the compulsory deposit insurance.
The report said that the figures were not final as it was not clear how much the CNB would reccover from the outstanding loans and assets of the closed-down banks.
"The extent of the expenditures will depend on the effectiovity of the management of obtained and remaining assets," the report said.

It said the total potential revenues from the dividends from state holdings in banks, the privatisation of the state shares, and the result of stimulation of investment demand and banks' income tax revenue -- exceeded the costs of the second phase and some of the first phase of the consolidation.
"The unprivatised stakes in the 'Big Four' have, considering standard sale on the capital market, the value exceeding 50 billion crowns," the report said.
The "Big Four" banks are Komercni Banka a.s. , IPB a.s. , Ceska Sporitelna a.s. , and Ceskoslovenska Obchodni Banka a.s. (CSOB).

Various state institutions and the Slovak central bank control about 90 percent of CSOB. The state holds through its privatisation agency, the National Property Fund, stakes rangiong from 29 to 48 percent in the other three banks.
"Only the sale of CSOB could bring a revenue correcponding to the total cost of this year's operations under the Consolidation Programme II," the report said.

"The total potential revenues, which are possible to be risen by the sale to strategic investors or by transferring to the macroeconomical level... highly exceed the costs of the Consolidation Programme II," it said.
